newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: YACHTING-DESERT SAILORS TAKE ON SYDNEY TO HOBART.
newsitem.headline: YACHTING-DESERT SAILORS TAKE ON SYDNEY TO HOBART.

text.p: They're called "Sandhill Sailors" as the nearest ocean is more than 1,500 km away and the closest thing to a wave is the slow moving sandhills of Australia's harsh Simpson Desert.

But the crew from the Alice Springs Yacht Club in the outback Northern Territory are serious yachties and have once again entered one the world's toughest ocean races -- the Sydney to Hobart starting on December 26.

After being forced to withdraw from the 630-nautical mile race in 1993 and 1994 because of damaged rigging, the desert sailors are determined to finish this year and have entered two leased boats, "Alice" and "The Spirit of Alice".

The idea to establish the Alice Springs Yacht Club and enter the Sydney-to-Hobart came over a drink at "The Oasis" bar in Alice Springs in 1993. Six months later the desert sailors were battling mountainous seas off Australia's east coast.

Initially ridiculed as a novelty that would probably not even get out of Sydney Harbour and dismissed as crazy by relatives and friends in Alice Springs, the desert sailors have since earned the respect of serious yachties.

"Most people thought we were a joke in 1993," says Alice crew member Michael McCauley, an American from Virginia state who works as a civilian engineer at the joint U.S.-Australian outback spy facility Pine Gap.

"They were surprised that we got so far," says McCauley, adding that The Spirit of Alice was one of 67 boats forced to retire from a fleet of 106 in a race battered by 11-metre (35-foot) seas and 70-knot gales.
Bob Barford, navigator on Alice, says attitudes towards them have changed from disbelief to respect.
"In 1993 we were looked at as a real novelty, a novelty without much yachting substance. But when we got so far the hats came off (in a salute) to us."

This year the two boats' crews of 16 have 20 Sydney-to-Hobart races' worth of experience. Landlocked Alice Springs, it seems, is a treasure trove of sailing knowledge, boasting round the world yachtsmen who have turned their back on the ocean.

"It's amazing how many yachties we have out in the desert," says Barford, who as a child sailed 18-footer dinghies on Sydney Harbour. "Many of the people I have known for years turned out to be sailors."
While the desert sailors probably only get to sail once a year, they say there is a direct relationship between ocean racing and outback living.

For Barford, a musican who supplements his income with surveying trips into the desert, the endless rolling sandhills which reach heights of six metres (19 feet) in the harsh Simpson Desert are like the rolling swells of the Pacific Ocean.
"Except for the colour, the formations are very similar -- long troughs and these rising hills," says Barford fondly remembering his desert home as he sits on a rocking boat in Sydney Harbour.
"At sunrise and sunset I emotionally make a connection. The textures are similar, you have these sand swells and these little wavelettes on top of the swell too," says Barford.
"It really does remind me of the ocean swell -- both are formed by winds and driven by the same sorts of pressure."
McCauley, who loves to prospect for semi-precious gems in the outback, agrees. He sees a parallel between survival in Australia's blisteringly hot outback and survival on the ocean.

"To me the outback is synonymous with being self-reliant. When you go fossicking (prospecting) you have to make sure you have enough water and tools and equipment in case you break down," says McCauley. "I feel as a sailor when I leave the dock I have to make sure I know how to handle emergencies and can respond accordingly."
The desert sailors say the loneliness of the outback, with its encircling horizon and imposing canopy of stars, and the fragile line between life and death is also similar to offshore sailing.
"There is a loneliness, but a real connection -- a belonging to the environment," says Barford of the desert and sailing.
"You have to sit neatly on the environment. Try and challenge it too much and it kills you, gobbles you up."
